content:
Webb County swung 26 points between the 2024 presidential election and the 2026 midterms — one of the sharpest reversals anywhere in Texas, according to new analysis from the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC).

President Donald Trump won 51% of the vote in Webb County in 2024. In 2026, Republican attorney general candidate Ken Paxton won just 25% here. That is a 26-point shift, LULAC Adelante PAC president Domingo Garcia told FOX 7 Austin.

Webb County was not alone. Across Texas' predominantly Latino counties, 72% of the collective vote went to the Democratic ticket, according to LULAC. Cameron County, home of Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, went from Trump 52% in 2024 to 30% for Paxton in 2026, with Hinojosa taking 70%. In Maverick County, where Trump won 59% in 2024, Paxton took just 28%.

A surge of new voters

About 1.6 million Latinos cast ballots in Texas this cycle, according to LULAC — nearly double the 900,000 who voted in the last midterm election. Of those voters, 400,000 were first-time Latino voters, and more than two-thirds of them were under the age of 30.

Organizers credited a massive mobilization effort. Somos Votantes invested more than $6 million in voter engagement and field organizing statewide, and LULAC spent upwards of $3 million on digital campaigns, direct messaging, and turnout drives. Somos Votantes teams knocked on close to 97,000 doors.

What drove the shift

Field teams reported that voters repeatedly cited everyday affordability — the cost of living, gas, grocery bills, and health care — alongside anxieties about community enforcement. "Latino voters, what they care about most is results," said Emmanuelle Leal-Santillan, media director for Somos Votantes. "They are not necessarily tied to one political party."

Garcia said the swing comes with a mandate: "The Democratic Party and its elected officials are gonna have to deliver to the working-class families of Texas and Tejanos. They have to make sure that the price of electricity goes down, the price of groceries and affordability goes down. The minimum wage in Texas hasn't been raised — it's still $7 an hour."

The same election returned Rep. Henry Cuellar to Congress in Texas' 28th District, as Webb Watch 956 previously reported. Laredo's own mayoral race, meanwhile, is still undecided: it heads to a Dec. 12 runoff between Alyssa Cigarroa and incumbent Victor Treviño.

Sources:

  • FOX 7 Austin — 2026 Election: Massive Latino turnout, border county reversal fuels Democratic wins
  • 2026 Laredo mayoral election results

title: Webb County Swung 26 Points in 2026 — What the Numbers Say
